exercises.prompt: Implement sumAll(arr) so it returns the sum of every number in arr, using Array.prototype.reduce. An empty array returns 0.
hints: reduce walks the array carrying a running result — here that result is a running total.
The callback takes the accumulator so far and the current element and returns the new total: (sum, x) => sum + x.
return arr.reduce((sum, x) => sum + x, 0) — the 0 both seeds the sum and is the empty-array answer.

exercises.prompt: Implement productAll(arr) so it returns the product of every number in arr, using reduce. By convention the product of an empty array is 1.
hints: Same fold as a sum, but combine the accumulator and each element with multiplication instead of addition.
A product accumulator must start at 1 — starting at 0 would make every answer 0.

exercises.prompt: Implement maxOf(arr) so it returns the largest number in arr, using reduce. Assume arr has at least one element. Note the values may all be negative.
hints: Fold the array while keeping the biggest value seen so far in the accumulator.
With no initial value, reduce uses the first element as the starting accumulator — ideal when the array is guaranteed non-empty.
return arr.reduce((max, x) => x > max ? x : max) — comparing values keeps it correct even when every number is negative.

exercises.prompt: Implement countPositive(arr) so it returns how many numbers in arr are strictly greater than zero, using reduce. Zero itself is not positive. An empty array returns 0.
hints: Reduce into a running count, adding 1 only for the elements that pass the test.
Add a conditional amount each step: count + (x > 0 ? 1 : 0).
return arr.reduce((count, x) => count + (x > 0 ? 1 : 0), 0) — strictly > 0, so zero is not counted.

exercises.prompt: Implement tally(arr), where arr is an array of strings, so it returns an object counting how many times each string appears — tally(['a', 'b', 'a']) is {a: 2, b: 1}. Use reduce with an object accumulator. An empty array returns an empty object {}.
hints: The accumulator here is an object that starts empty ({}) and gains a key the first time each string shows up.
For each string x, set counts[x] to its previous count plus one — counts[x] = (counts[x] || 0) + 1 — where || 0 handles the first sighting.
Inside the reducer, update counts[x] then return counts so the next step keeps building the same object; seed the reduce with {}.
